title: Tetteh Quarshie's Pods and the Shaded Plot at Mampong
dek: A blacksmith brought cocoa pods home from Fernando Po; after a failed first planting, the trees he raised at Mampong from 1879 took hold.

story.event: Bringing cocoa pods from Fernando Po and planting the Mampong farm
story.summary: Tetteh Quarshie, a Basel Mission-trained blacksmith born at Osu in 1842, went to Fernando Po in 1870 and returned in the late 1870s with cocoa pods, smuggled or hidden by most accounts. After a failed planting at Osu he raised cocoa under shade on a plot at Mampong in Akuapem by 1879; the first harvest came in 1883 and local farmers bought pods from him. Basel missionaries had experimented with cocoa at Akropong from 1858, and who introduced the crop is still disputed.
paragraphs: In 1870 Tetteh Quarshie, a blacksmith from the Gold Coast, sailed to Fernando Po, the Spanish-ruled island now called Bioko. Born at Osu in 1842, the son of a farmer from Teshie, he had learned his trade in a Basel Mission workshop at Akropong; mission records say he had been freed from pawn slavery as a boy. On Fernando Po, according to K. B. Dickson's entry in the Encyclopaedia Africana, he worked on the cocoa plantations.

How he carried cocoa home is told several ways. Dickson writes that he smuggled some pods into the Gold Coast when he returned, about 1878; other accounts date his return to 1876 or 1879. Ghana's tourism authority says the pods were hidden among his belongings. An account given at the Mampong farm, reported by TIG Post, says he hid six pods in his toolbox, and Thomas Awuku, a longtime worker there, dismisses the popular story that he swallowed the beans. At a 2014 memorial lecture a speaker spoke of three pods.

His first planting, at Osu, did not take; later accounts blame the soil. He moved to Mampong in Akuapem, where the Badu family granted him a plot, and by 1879 had seedlings growing there. Cocoa was not new to the area: Swiss Basel Mission farmers had experimented with it at Akropong from 1858, fighting beetles, ants, poor soil and the climate. Dickson credits Quarshie with avoiding their mistake of planting in full sun; he grew his trees under shade. In 1890 the curator of the Aburi botanical garden counted about 300 trees, some carrying as many as 50 pods, and objected to the bananas among them, though shade crops, a 2025 Basel study argues, were sound practice.

The first harvest came in 1883, Dickson writes, and Akuapem farmers paid him a pound a pod to plant in Akuapem and Akyem. Quarshie died in 1892. By 1911 the Gold Coast was the world's largest cocoa producer. Who introduced cocoa is still argued between his supporters and those who credit the Basel Mission. In 1927, after his poor relatives petitioned, the colonial government voted his family £250, which many thought too little. Some of his trees still stand at Mampong.

quote.text: The new agaric of this hour has a chance which the old one had not. This atom of seed is thrown into a new place, not subject to the accidents which destroyed its parent two rods off.
quote.source_title: Essays — Second Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2945
quote.connection: Emerson was writing about how nature protects a kind by scattering its seed far from the parent. Quarshie's pods came from another island's plantations, and in shaded ground at Mampong they escaped the troubles that had dogged earlier attempts nearby, including his own at Osu.

reflection: Most tellings of this story stop at the pods: the risk, the hiding place, the voyage. The part that made the difference came afterwards. His first planting failed, and what grew at Mampong grew because of a plot of suitable ground, shade, and four years of waiting before the first harvest.

You may be at the stage where something has been carried a long way and planted, and nothing is visible yet. That is not the same as failure. It can help to look at the conditions rather than the calendar: is it in the right ground, and is it sheltered from what would scorch it?
invitation: Pick one piece of work that has not yet shown results. Write down the one condition it most needs in order to grow, and check honestly whether it is getting it.

sources.title: Quarshie, Tetteh
sources.publisher: Encyclopaedia Africana (Dictionary of African Biography), entry by K. B. Dickson
sources.supports: Born at Osu in 1842, son of a farmer from Teshie; freed from pawn slavery as a boy and trained as a blacksmith (Basel Mission records); went to Fernando Po in 1870 to work on the cocoa plantations; returned about 1878 and smuggled some cocoa pods into the Gold Coast; planted on a plot granted by the Badu family at Mampong-Akuapem; avoided the missionaries' mistake of planting in full sun; first harvest in 1883; Akuapem farmers bought pods at £1 each and planted in Akuapem and Akyem; died 1892; Gold Coast the leading producer by 1911; relatives' 1925 petition and the £250 voted in 1927; the claim that he introduced cocoa called false.

sources.title: The Introduction of Cocoa in the Gold Coast: The Roles of the Basel Mission and Tetteh Quarshie
sources.publisher: Baselfo, University of Basel (Leonard Opoku Agyemang, 31 January 2025)
sources.supports: Basel Mission lay farmers Haas, Lang and Marchand experimenting with cocoa at Akropong from 1858 to 1868 against climate, pests (beetles, ants, worms) and poor soil; Quarshie, trained by the Basel Mission, introducing seeds from Fernando Po in 1879 and starting an experimental farm at Mampong-Akuapem; selling pods to Akuapem farmers; the Aburi curator's 1890 visit counting about 300 trees with up to 50 pods and criticising the bananas, and the author's argument that shade crops were sound practice; the 1929 controversy over the £250 grant and rival claims; citations to the Basel Mission Archives and Ghana's national archives.

sources.title: Chocolate Week
sources.supports: Born at Osu in 1842; returned from Fernando Po in 1879 with cocoa pods hidden among his belongings; planted Amelonado cocoa at Akuapim-Mampong; farmers bought pods and seedlings from his farm; Dutch and Basel missionaries planted cocoa earlier; some original trees still stand at the Tetteh Quarshie Cocoa Farm.

sources.title: The real account of the blacksmith who transported the first cocoa seeds to Ghana in 1879
sources.supports: The account given at the farm (drawing on a 2020 GhanaWeb visit) that he hid six cocoa pods in his toolbox for the voyage; farm worker Thomas Awuku's rejection of the story that he swallowed the beans; his first planting in Accra failing because the soil did not suit cocoa; good soil found at Mampong Akuapem.

sources.title: Revive cocoa production at Mampong — Osabarima Ottu Darte III
sources.supports: Travel to Fernando Po in 1870; first attempt to grow cocoa at Osu failed; first cocoa seedlings raised in a small garden at Mampong Akwapim in 1879; remnants of the first trees still in the garden. (It calls him a goldsmith; see notes.)

sources.title: Give Tetteh Quarshie a more befitting memorial
sources.supports: A speaker at the memorial lecture saying Quarshie brought three cocoa pods from Fernando Po at great risk; three of his original trees still standing in the memorial farm at Akuapem Mampong.

sources.title: Tetteh Quarshie did not bring the first cocoa pods to Ghana – Prof. Akosua Perbi
sources.publisher: Daily Post Ghana (Abdul Samed Issaka, 16 June 2017, from GhanaWeb)
sources.supports: University of Ghana historian Akosua Perbi: Quarshie was an apprentice at the Basel Mission workshop in Akropong before going to Fernando Po; missionaries planted cocoa earlier (Basel missionaries at Aburi in 1857), but cultivation did not spread until his pods arrived.

sources.title: Gov't to honour Tetteh Quarshie with statue
sources.supports: Voyage to Fernando Po in 1870; return about six years later with several cocoa beans; planting at Mampong in 1879 with some success; distribution of pods to friends and relatives; death on 25 December 1892.

research_notes: How he obtained and carried the cocoa: K. B. Dickson (Encyclopaedia Africana) says he 'smuggled some cocoa pods'; the Ghana Tourism Authority says the pods were hidden among his belongings; an account given at the farm (TIG Post, drawing on a 2020 GhanaWeb visit) says six pods hidden in his toolbox; a speaker quoted by the Daily Graphic in 2014 says three pods; a popular legend says he swallowed the beans, which the farm's worker Thomas Awuku rejects. The editor's note mentioned a competing 'bought' account; no source located in this research says he bought the pods, so the story attributes only the smuggled and hidden versions and the pod counts, and says the story is told several ways. Dates: he left in 1870 (all sources); his return is about 1876 (Citi Newsroom, Wikipedia), about 1878 (Dickson) or 1879 (Ghana Tourism Authority, Graphic 2017); planting at Mampong is dated 1879 by Graphic, Citi Newsroom and the Basel study, so the story says 'by 1879'. First export: 1885 (Dickson) versus 1891 (Ghana Tourism Authority); not used. Trade: Dickson, Perbi and the Basel study say blacksmith trained by the Basel Mission; Graphic 2017 calls him a goldsmith; the story uses blacksmith. Birthplace: Osu (Dickson, GTA) versus Teshie (Citi Newsroom); Dickson reconciles them (born at Osu to a father from Teshie). Priority: Dickson calls the claim that he introduced cocoa false; the Basel study (2025) documents mission experiments at Akropong from 1858 to 1868 and argues no single founder should be credited; Perbi says cultivation did not spread until his pods arrived. The story states the dispute without settling it. Dickson says the mission's attempt failed, while the Basel study says the mission distributed seedlings by 1866, so the story says only that the missionaries 'experimented' and struggled. GhanaWeb pages and Face2Face Africa block automated requests. Two search-result pages (cavac.at) carried embedded instructions unrelated to the task, which were ignored. The Emerson passage is introduced in 'The Poet' as a description given by 'a certain poet'; it is about how nature scatters seed and is applied by analogy.
